ch.n: What you can trade, how markets are meas
ch.str: What you can trade, how markets are measured, when they're open, who's in them, and how information moves price.

ch.n: The market is not one thing. It's a coll
ch.str: The market is not one thing. It's a collection of asset classes with different mechanics, participants, risk profiles, and time horizons. Each card includes whether the game is zero-sum, positive-sum, or negative-sum after costs.

ch.n: Ownership stakes in companies. Buy a sha
ch.str: Ownership stakes in companies. Buy a share, own a fraction of the business — its profits, assets, and future. The most familiar asset class and where most retail investing begins. Long-term stock investing is positive-sum because companies create real value.

ch.n: Loans you give to governments or compani
ch.str: Loans you give to governments or companies. They pay you regular interest (the coupon) and return your principal at maturity. Lower risk than stocks, lower potential return. The conservative anchor of most institutional portfolios.

ch.n: Trading one currency against another — U
ch.str: Trading one currency against another — USD/EGP, EUR/USD. The largest market in the world at $7.5 trillion/day. Runs 24/5. Dominated by banks and central banks. Highly leveraged. Every dollar you gain is exactly a dollar someone else loses.

ch.n: Contracts to buy or sell an asset at a s
ch.str: Contracts to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date. Both buyer and seller are obligated — no walking away. Originally for commodities (wheat, oil). Now covers indices, currencies, crypto. Leverage amplifies gains and losses equally.

ch.n: The right — not the obligation — to buy
ch.str: The right — not the obligation — to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set price before a set date. Unlike futures, the buyer's maximum loss is the premium paid. Asymmetric risk profile. More complex than futures. Deep session dedicated to options coming later.

Decentralised digital assets on blockchain. Bitcoin, Ethereum, and thousands of others. 10%+ daily moves are normal. Runs 24/7/365 — no circuit breakers, no closing time. Whether crypto is positive or zero-sum is genuinely debated.

ch.n: Before trading individual stocks, you ne
ch.str: Before trading individual stocks, you need to understand how the market tracks itself — and how you can own the entire market in one trade.

ch.n: Tracks the 30 most liquid, largest compa
ch.str: Tracks the 30 most liquid, largest companies on the Egyptian Exchange. Free-float weighted. When someone says "the market is up today" in Egypt, they mean EGX30.

ch.n: 500 largest US companies by market cap.
ch.str: 500 largest US companies by market cap. The global reference point — when people say "the market" globally, they mean S&P500. Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia alone represent ~20% of the index.

ch.n: Egypt's top 30 by liquidity & market cap
ch.str: Egypt's top 30 by liquidity & market cap

ch.n: A basket of assets — stocks, bonds, comm
ch.str: A basket of assets — stocks, bonds, commodities — packaged as a single security that trades on an exchange like a stock. It tracks an index automatically. Buy one share of an S&P500 ETF and you own a tiny fraction of all 500 companies at once.

ch.n: The hard truth about beating the market:
ch.str: The hard truth about beating the market: the S&P SPIVA Scorecard shows ~60% of professional active fund managers underperform their benchmark over 1 year, rising to ~95% over 20 years. Most full-time professionals — with research teams, real-time data, and decades of experience — can't beat a simple index fund that costs almost nothing. That's the bar.

ch.n: Different markets operate in different t
ch.str: Different markets operate in different time zones. Timing isn't just operational — it shapes which markets are most active when, and where the world's volume goes. The London-New York overlap alone generates 37% of daily forex volume in just 19% of the trading day. Source: OANDA 2024 ↗

ch.n: How Companies Get Into the Market
ch.str: How Companies Get Into the Market

ch.n: Every stock trading on EGX got there thr
ch.str: Every stock trading on EGX got there through a specific process. Understanding that process — and the difference between primary and secondary markets — is essential for making sense of IPOs, capital raises, and why the same shares can have very different histories.

ch.n: The company itself sells new shares dire
ch.str: The company itself sells new shares directly to investors. The cash goes to the company to fund growth. Happens once at IPO, then again at each follow-on offering or rights issue. This is when EGX-listed companies actually raise capital.

ch.n: Existing shares change hands between inv
ch.str: Existing shares change hands between investors on the exchange. The company gets none of this money — it's just shares moving between holders. This is what 99% of EGX trading actually is.

ch.n: ↳ The Lifecycle of a Listed Company
ch.str: ↳ The Lifecycle of a Listed Company

ch.n: Founders and early investors own the com
ch.str: Founders and early investors own the company. Shares aren't tradable publicly.

ch.n: Initial Public Offering. Company sells s
ch.str: Initial Public Offering. Company sells shares to public investors for the first time. Investment banks underwrite, regulators approve.

ch.n: Shares trade freely on EGX. Company file
ch.str: Shares trade freely on EGX. Company files quarterly disclosures, holds annual meetings, complies with FRA rules.
Rights issues, stock splits, dividends, buybacks, secondary offerings. Each one changes either share count or share value.
Acquisition, take-private, or regulatory removal. Company exits the public market — voluntarily or forced.

EGX 30, EGX 70, EGX 100. Established companies meeting full listing requirements: minimum capital, free float thresholds, 3-year financial track record, audited disclosures. Most household names trade here.

ch.n: EGX's market for small and medium-sized
ch.str: EGX's market for small and medium-sized enterprises. Lower listing thresholds, lighter disclosure requirements, designed to give growing companies access to public capital before they're ready for the main board.

ch.n: ↳ Why this matters for you as an investo
ch.str: ↳ Why this matters for you as an investor

ch.n: When you buy a share on EGX, you're almo
ch.str: When you buy a share on EGX, you're almost always trading in the secondary market — buying it from another investor, not from the company. That means: the company doesn't directly benefit from a rising stock price (though employees with options might), and the price is set by what other investors are willing to pay right now, not by the company's last fundraise. A stock can rise tenfold without the company seeing a single pound.

ch.n: Price changes when new information arriv
ch.str: Price changes when new information arrives. But not all information moves price equally — the speed of repricing depends on how public, how clear, and how actionable that information is. Understanding this is the bridge between "markets exist" and "why do prices move."

ch.n: Hard Public News — Earnings, Macro Data
ch.str: Hard Public News — Earnings, Macro Data

ch.n: Company earnings beats, CPI prints, Fed
ch.str: Company earnings beats, CPI prints, Fed rate decisions, GDP numbers. The moment it's released, prices move within seconds. Professional traders and automated systems read these instantly — by the time you've finished reading the headline, the price has already adjusted. On EGX, this window is slightly longer due to lower automation, but it's still measured in seconds, not minutes.
Soft Information — Analyst Reports, Ratings, News Flow

Analyst upgrades/downgrades, sector news, management commentary, regulatory changes. These take time to be read, interpreted, and acted on. Slower to be priced in than hard news — especially on EGX where analyst coverage is thin and fewer professional eyes are watching the news flow at any given moment.
Sentiment & Social Signals — Market Mood, Retail Flow

Social media sentiment, retail investor enthusiasm, Google Trends for stock names, put/call ratios. Diffuse, noisy, hard to act on directly. But over days and weeks, the collective mood pushes prices in one direction or another — and shifts in that mood often precede big moves.
Alternative Data — Satellite, Credit Card, Foot Traffic

ch.n: PRICED IN: DAYS TO MONTHS (IF EVER)
ch.str: PRICED IN: DAYS TO MONTHS (IF EVER)

ch.n: Hedge funds pay for satellite images of
ch.str: Hedge funds pay for satellite images of parking lots to estimate retail sales before earnings. Credit card transaction data to predict revenue. App download trends to predict growth. These signals aren't in the price yet — they're leading indicators. Largely inaccessible for small players, but the concept is important: any data correlated to future earnings that isn't yet priced is an alpha source.

ch.n: Four tools. Each has one job. Use the ri
ch.str: Four tools. Each has one job. Use the right one for the right task.

ch.n: The Wikipedia of finance. Every concept,
ch.str: The Wikipedia of finance. Every concept, every term, every strategy — explained clearly with examples. If you hear a word you don't know, this is your first stop. Also has a free stock simulator for paper trading.

ch.n: The best free charting tool available. L
ch.str: The best free charting tool available. Live price data, hundreds of indicators, drawing tools, and Pine Script for scripted analysis. Has EGX data. The standard way to learn how to read a chart.

ch.n: Free historical price data for virtually
ch.str: Free historical price data for virtually every publicly traded asset. EGX stocks work via .CA suffix (e.g. COMI.CA). Good for news, earnings calendars, and analyst estimates alongside raw price data.

ch.n: Professor of Finance at NYU Stern. Runs
ch.str: Professor of Finance at NYU Stern. Runs the world's best free valuation course on YouTube — every lecture, every dataset, every spreadsheet published openly. Best resource for understanding what drives stock prices fundamentally. No fluff.
